messages.subject: Re: Comparison line transect and point transect--subject change
parts:
Jim:

A good place to get a reminder of how to enter data (whether line or
point transects), is to look at the sample projects that come with
Distance. The 'Sample Projects' directory is the default directory that
Distance will examine when you ask to open a project.

For your specific question regarding point transects with no detections,
take a look at the project 'Songbird.dst' When you look at the data
sheet for that project, you will note that point 17 had no detections.
It has a record at the sample layer (called Point transect), but no
associated records in the observation layer. There needs to be a record
associated with the point, because you exerted sampling effort, even if
you did not record any detections.

Hope that helps. Let me know if that answers your question.

CASAER, Jim wrote:
> > Hey
> > During the training we shortly toughed the problem of observation points
> > (points sampling) without observations, now I'm focussing the problem in
> > reality, I do not remember how to enter the data in the data sheet
> >
> > Please advise ?
> > Jim
> >
> >
> > -----Oorspronkelijk bericht-----
> > Van: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
> > [mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] Namens Steve Buckland
> > Verzonden: donderdag 30 april 2009 13:05
> > Aan: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
> > Onderwerp: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Comparison line transect and point transect
> >
> > Johanna, I think the problem is more to do with the design than the
> > method. You should get comparable abundance estimates - and you do,
> > when you take account of the very wide confidence interval for lines.
> > That is unsurprising, when you consider your design has just 3 lines.
> > That is far too few. (In the 2001 book, we say 'a minimum of 10-20
> > lines'.) If you can fit 72 points into your survey region, you can
> > certainly fit more than 3 lines in.
> >
> > You should also use laser rangefinders, as measurement errors in point
> > transect sampling can generate substantial upward bias in the abundance
> > estimate - and your point transect abundance estimate is higher here
> > than your line transect estimate.
> >
> > Steve Buckland
> >
> > Johanna Reinhard wrote:
> >

>> >>

>> >>
